publication_scope.blurb: Louis Le Blanc de Beaulieu - Sedan Theological Theses, newly rendered from the 1675 London Latin. Covers De Theologia through Angelorum & Hominum Sanctorum Cultu Romana I-LXXVII and Pars Secunda (Reformata) I-CI, De Primi Hominis Immortalitate I-XXXV, De Justitia Primi Hominis I-LIX, De Libero Hominis Arbitrio in genere I-XLVIII, De Libero Hominis Arbitrio absolute & in se spectato (Scholae Romanae doctrina I-XLIX; Pars Tertia I-XLIII), the theses on reconciling divine concurrence with human freedom I-LIX, on human freedom and divine foreknowledge I-XLIV, and on human freedom and the divine decrees, Part One (middle knowledge) I-LXV, Part Two (the Roman doctors) I-XXXVI and Part Three (the Reformed) I-LI, and on how fallen man's free choice stands toward saving good (I-LX), and on the necessity of grace for moral good in fallen man (Pars Prior I-LIII; Pars Posterior, the Protestant doctrine, I-LIX), and on the various distinctions and senses of grace in the Roman School (I-LXX) and in the Reformed Schools (I-XLIX), and on the Roman School's division of grace into sufficient and efficacious (I-LXXXIX). Not the collected folio.
publication_scope.era_note: Le Blanc wrote in the mid-seventeenth century as Reformed professor at the Academy of Sedan. This is not a patristic work. It is a public-domain Latin Reformed retrieval on the same Fathers-site pipeline. The 1675 Pitt folio is Public Domain Mark 1.0. Do not treat the site as ante-Nicene only.

source_text: LXXIII. Quod attinet autem gratiam efficacem, Thomistae cum Jansenio docent nullam esse Christi gratiam quae ratione quadam efficax non sit, hoc est, quae non producat certo & infallibiliter effectum aliquem, ad quem efficiendum praecise a Deo data est, & absoluto Dei decreto destinata. Jansenius vero cum illis agnoscit gratiam Christi, non moraliter tantum, sed etiam physice voluntatem determinare. Ac communi consensu, & pari contentione, pertendunt utrique gratiam divinam ex se & per se efficacem esse: ejus efficaciam a consensu liberi arbitrii non pendere, sed esse absolutam: & gratiam libero arbitrio dominari, non vero potestati illius subjacere.
english: Thesis LXXIII. On efficacious grace, the Thomists teach together with Jansenius that no grace of Christ exists that is not efficacious in some respect: there is none that fails to bring about, surely and infallibly, some effect, the very effect for which God precisely gives it and to which his absolute decree has destined it. Jansenius, for his part, grants with them that Christ's grace determines the will physically as well as morally.

With one accord and equal insistence both sides maintain that divine grace is efficacious from itself and of itself. Its efficacy is absolute and does not hang on the consent of free choice, and grace is master over free choice rather than subject to its power.

source_text: LXXIV. Caeterum circa naturam gratiae efficacis in multis dissentiunt: ut prolixe notat & refert Jansenius de gratia Christi salvatoris libro octavo capite primo. Nam Thomistis recentioribus gratia voluntatem physice praedeterminans, ut supra fuit expositum, est motio quaedam virtuosa, quae habet esse quoddam incompletum; & in voluntate est per modum quo colores sunt in aere, & impetus in re quae impellitur. Jansenio vero gratia illa est affectio realis & vera voluntatis, consistens in amore & desiderio quodam boni coelestis & spiritualis, quo suaviter & cum ingenti jucunditate sursum rapitur animus humanus. Ac proinde Thomistis efficax istud auxilium in voluntate tantum passive recipitur, Jansenio vero est quid active ab ea procedens, & motus illius vitalis.
english: Thesis LXXIV. On the nature of efficacious grace, however, they differ in many respects, as Jansenius notes and reports at length in De gratia Christi Salvatoris, book 8, chapter 1. For the recent Thomists, the grace that physically predetermines the will is, as explained above, a 'virtual motion' with a kind of incomplete being, present in the will in the way colours are present in the air and impetus in a thing that has been pushed.

For Jansenius, that grace is a real and true affection of the will, consisting in a love and desire for heavenly and spiritual good, by which the human mind is carried upward sweetly and with immense joy. So for the Thomists this efficacious aid is only received passively in the will, while for Jansenius it is something that proceeds actively from the will and is a vital movement of it.

source_text: LXXV. Deinde juxta Thomistarum mentem, auxilium Physice praedeterminans tale est, ut in quibuscunque circumstantiis voluntas collocetur, semper faciat facere, & operetur effectum suum, omnemque superet resistentiam. Nempe si idem auxilium, quod hunc vel illum hominem ad bene operandum movet & determinat, reliquis omnibus daretur, omnes similiter moveret, adeoque hunc ipsum quibuscunque supponeretur concupiscentiae motibus agitatus. Verum, ex Jansenii sensu, aliter se habet Christi adjutorium efficax. Nam delectatio victrix, in qua adjutorium illud collocat, relativa est. Tunc enim est victrix quando delectatione opposita major est. Quod si contingat alteram ardentiorem esse, in solis inefficacibus desideriis haerebit animus, nec efficaciter unquam volet quod volendum est. Proinde quae in uno victrix est, propter debiliores concupiscentiae motus, in alio superabitur & inefficax erit, propter motus ejusdem concupiscentiae vehementiores. Nec quae in hoc homine ad vincendam praesentem tentationem sufficit, sufficiet alio tempore, si fortior & acrior urgeat tentatio.
english: Thesis LXXV. Next, in the Thomists' view the physically predetermining aid is such that, whatever the circumstances in which the will is placed, it always makes it act, produces its effect, and overcomes all resistance. If the same aid that moves and determines this or that person to act well were given to everyone else, it would move them all alike, and would move this same person too, whatever impulses of concupiscence he were supposed to be shaken by.

In Jansenius's sense, however, Christ's efficacious aid works otherwise. The victorious delight in which he places that aid is relative: it is victorious only when it is greater than the opposing delight. If the other delight happens to be more ardent, the mind will cling only to ineffective desires and will never effectively will what ought to be willed.

So a delight that wins in one person, because the impulses of concupiscence are weaker, will be overcome and prove inefficacious in another, because the impulses of the same concupiscence are more violent. Nor will what is enough for this person to overcome a present temptation be enough at another time, if a stronger and fiercer temptation presses on him.

source_text: LXXVI. Praeterea physicam praedeterminationem voluntati humanae ad bene operandum necessariam esse, ideo existimant Thomistae recentiores, quod voluntas, ut omnes reliquae causae secundae, opus habet a Deo causa prima praemoveri, ut actu operetur. Atque etiam illam necessitatem petunt a voluntatis indifferentia, quam propterea necesse sit a causa superiori ad agendum determinari. Sed Jansenius non alia de causa gratiae divinae auxilium efficax humanae voluntati necessarium putat, quam propter vulnus a peccato inflictum, & infirmitatem ex concupiscentia homini lapso adhaerente contractam.
english: Thesis LXXVI. Further, the recent Thomists hold that physical predetermination is necessary for the human will to act well because the will, like all other secondary causes, needs to be premoved by God, the First Cause, in order actually to act. They also derive this necessity from the will's indifference, which on that account must be determined to act by a higher cause.

Jansenius, however, thinks the efficacious aid of divine grace necessary to the human will for one reason only: the wound inflicted by sin, and the weakness contracted from the concupiscence that clings to fallen man.

source_text: LXXVII. Ac proinde, secundum Thomistarum hypotheses, auxilium physice praedeterminans necessarium fuit, homini etiam integro, & citra ullam peccati considerationem. Sed juxta Jansenium, adjutorium efficax, quo fit ut homo velit & operetur, nullum locum habuit in statu innocentiae; Sed solum adjutorium sine quo homo quidem bene agere non poterat; & cum quo poterat facile consistere, ut homo bene non ageret; Utpote quod libero arbitrio subdebatur, minime vero liberum hominis arbitrium sibi subjiciebat.
english: Thesis LXXVII. On the Thomists' assumptions, then, the physically predetermining aid was necessary even for man unfallen, quite apart from any thought of sin. On Jansenius's view, by contrast, the efficacious aid by which a person comes to will and act had no place in the state of innocence.

There was only the aid without which man could not act well, and which could easily coexist with his not acting well, since it was subject to free choice and in no way brought man's free choice under itself.

source_text: LXXVIII. Caeterum a sententia Jansenii Iprensis, & recentiorum etiam Thomistarum, multum distat doctrina Ludovici Molinae Jesuitae celeberrimi, quem plures alii sequuntur. Quod ut clarius pateat, summa sententiae illius, circa gratiam efficacem atque sufficientem, ex scriptis ejus est breviter repetenda. Ille ergo non vult ullum gratiae auxilium sufficiens dici, praeter illud, quo posito, nihil amplius ex parte Dei praerequiritur, ut actio reapse sequatur. Atque hoc modo sufficiens gratiae auxilium docet a Deo concedi, tam iis qui bene non agunt, neque se ad Deum convertunt, quam iis qui convertuntur & bene operantur.
english: Thesis LXXVIII. The teaching of the most celebrated Jesuit Luis de Molina, whom many others follow, is far removed from the view of Jansenius of Ypres and of the recent Thomists as well. To make this clearer, the substance of his view on efficacious and sufficient grace should be briefly restated from his writings.

He will not have any aid of grace called sufficient except one which, once given, requires nothing further on God's part for the action actually to follow. In this sense he teaches that God grants sufficient aid of grace both to those who do not act well and do not turn to God and to those who are converted and act well.

source_text: LXXIX. Inde est quod auxilium sufficiens dividit in auxilium efficax, & auxilium inefficax. Auxilium efficax est quod sequitur effectus, id est, bonum opus ad quod hominem movet. Inefficax vero quod caret effectu, & per quod homo actu non convertitur, nec bene operatur.
english: Thesis LXXIX. Hence he divides sufficient aid into efficacious and inefficacious aid. Efficacious aid is the aid that its effect follows, that is, the good work to which it moves a person. Inefficacious aid lacks its effect: through it a person is not actually converted and does not act well.

source_text: LXXX. Ut autem auxilium sit efficax, non pendet, juxta ipsum, ex peculiari Dei motione, qua posita semper consentiat & cooperetur liberum arbitrium, remota vero nunquam consentiat aut cooperetur. Imo qui ita sentiunt, errare putat in fide. Postquam enim retulit sententiam eorum, qui dicunt ipsi auxilio Dei, sive Deo efficaciter, aut inefficaciter per illud moventi, tribuendum esse quod liberum arbitrium consentiat, aut non consentiat: ita ut quoties Deus moverit per auxilium, quod ex modo motionis divinae, atque ex Deo ipso habet quod sit efficax, liberum arbitrium consentiat, & cooperetur ad salutem; quod si moverit per auxilium, quod ab eo non habet ut sit efficax, liberum arbitrium non consentiat, nec cooperetur ad salutem: subjungit, Certe non dubitarem sententiam hanc, hoc modo explicatam, errorem in fide appellare. Ratio autem ejus est, quod ita ipsi sic perire videtur arbitrii libertas: quia, scilicet, hominis conversio & perseverantia, non ab innata & propria ejus libertate pendebit, sed a qualitate auxilii & motionis divinae. Si namque, inquit, arbitrium nostrum ab efficacia auxilii divini habet quod consentiat, aut non consentiat Deo vocanti, & cooperetur, aut non cooperetur ad salutem, perseveretque aut non perseveret in gratia, certe non ab innata & propria libertate id pendet, sed a qualitate auxilii & motionis divinae; atque adeo neque est quod illi cedat in laudem & meritum, quin potius perit omnino libertas arbitrii ad salutem. Libro de Concordia liberi arbitrii cum gratiae Donis &c. Quaestione 23. Articulo 4. & 5. disputat. 1. membro 6.
english: Thesis LXXX. On his view, an aid's being efficacious does not depend on a special motion of God which, once given, always brings free choice to consent and cooperate, and which, once withdrawn, leaves it never consenting or cooperating. Indeed he thinks those who hold this err in faith.

He reports the view of those who say that free choice's consenting or not consenting is to be ascribed to God's aid itself, or to God moving efficaciously or inefficaciously through it: so that whenever God moves through an aid that has its efficacy from the manner of the divine motion and from God himself, free choice consents and cooperates toward salvation, and whenever he moves through an aid that does not have its efficacy from him, free choice does not consent or cooperate toward salvation. Then he adds: 'I would certainly not hesitate to call this view, explained in this way, an error in faith.'

His reason is that in this way, as he sees it, freedom of choice is lost, since a person's conversion and perseverance will then depend not on his own innate freedom but on the quality of the aid and of the divine motion. 'For if,' he says, 'our choice has from the efficacy of the divine aid that it consents or does not consent to God's call, cooperates or does not cooperate toward salvation, and perseveres or does not persevere in grace, then this certainly depends not on its own innate freedom but on the quality of the aid and of the divine motion; and so there is nothing that could be credited to it for praise and merit, but rather freedom of choice toward salvation is lost altogether.' Concordia liberi arbitrii cum gratiae donis, question 23, articles 4-5, disputation 1, member 6.

source_text: LXXXI. Itaque, ex illius mente, Divisio auxilii sufficientis, in efficax & inefficax, sumitur ab effectu, qui ab arbitrii libertate pendet. Adeoque penes humanum arbitrium situm est, & in illius potestate positum, ut auxilium gratiae, quod ex se sufficiens est, vel fit efficax, vel maneat inefficax. Illudque auxilium sufficiens efficax dicitur, cum quo arbitrium pro sua libertate convertitur, cum tamen, nihil ex auxilio impediente, potuerit non converti, idque in sensu composito, non tantum in sensu diviso: illud vero inefficax dicitur, cum quo arbitrium, pro eadem sua libertate, non convertitur, cum tamen potuerit converti, & absque ullo alio gratiae Dei auxilio reapse & de facto, conversionis actum elicere. Asserimus, inquit, auxilia praevenientis atque adjuvantis gratiae, quae lege ordinaria viatoribus conceduntur, quod efficacia, aut inefficacia ad conversionem, seu justificationem sint, pendere a libero consensu & cooperatione arbitrii nostri cum illis, atque adeo in libera potestate nostra esse, vel illa efficacia reddere, consentiendo & cooperando cum illis, ad actus quibus ad justificationem disponimur, vel inefficacia illa reddere, continendo consensum & cooperationem nostram, aut etiam eliciendo contrarium dissensum. Ejusdem libri quaest. 14. art. 13. disp. 40.
english: Thesis LXXXI. On his view, then, the division of sufficient aid into efficacious and inefficacious is taken from the effect, and the effect depends on the freedom of choice. So it lies with human choice, and is placed in its power, whether the aid of grace, sufficient of itself, becomes efficacious or remains inefficacious.

Sufficient aid is called efficacious when choice is converted with it by its own freedom, although, with nothing in the aid preventing it, choice could have remained unconverted, and that in the composite sense and not only in the divided sense. It is called inefficacious when choice, by the same freedom, is not converted with it, although it could have been converted and could actually and in fact have elicited the act of conversion without any further aid of God's grace.

'We assert,' he says, 'that whether the aids of prevenient and assisting grace granted by the ordinary law to those still on their pilgrimage are efficacious or inefficacious for conversion or justification depends on the free consent and cooperation of our choice with them. It is therefore in our free power either to make them efficacious, by consenting and cooperating with them toward the acts by which we are disposed for justification, or to make them inefficacious, by withholding our consent and cooperation, or even by eliciting the contrary dissent.' Same book, question 14, article 13, disputation 40.

source_text: LXXXII. Igitur secundum illius hypotheses, auxilium efficax & auxilium inefficax, ab eventu sic denominantur: nec auxilium efficax quicquam in se plus habet quam auxilium inefficax. Adeoque contingere potest & saepe etiam contingit, ut ex duobus aequali gratia Dei praeventis, unus convertatur, alter non convertatur. Quinimo quandoque accidit, ut qui majora gratiae auxilia acceperit, maneat impoenitens, aut negligat bene operari: Ille vero cui Deus pauciora & minora auxilia concesserit, veram poenitentiam agat, & studeat bonis operibus; quia prior uti noluerit gratia illa majore sibi a Deo concessa, alter vero minore gratia, pro sua libertate, bene usus fuerit. Ac etiam aliquando fit, ut ex duobus in quibus gratia efficax est, ille qui minore gratia adjuvatur, ferventius & majore cum zelo operetur; ille vero qui majori, languidius atque remissius.
english: Thesis LXXXII. On his assumptions, then, efficacious and inefficacious aid are so named from the outcome, and efficacious aid has nothing more in itself than inefficacious aid. It can therefore happen, and often does, that of two people anticipated by equal grace from God one is converted and the other is not.

Indeed it sometimes happens that someone who has received greater aids of grace remains impenitent or neglects to act well, while another, to whom God has granted fewer and lesser aids, truly repents and is eager for good works, because the first refused to use the greater grace God granted him and the second, in his freedom, made good use of the lesser.

It also sometimes happens that of two people in whom grace is efficacious, the one helped by lesser grace acts more fervently and with greater zeal, while the one helped by greater grace acts more sluggishly and slackly.

source_text: LXXXIII. Haec est expressa Molinae doctrina quaestionis 14. articulo 13. disputatione 12. Fieri potest, inquit, ut duorum, qui aequali auxilio interius a Deo vocantur, unus pro libertate sui arbitrii convertatur, & alter in infidelitate permaneat: saepe etiam accidit, ut cum quo auxilio unus non convertitur, alius convertatur. Imo fieri potest, ut aliquis praeventus & vocatus longe majori auxilio, pro sua libertate non convertatur, & alius cum longe minori convertatur. Saepe enim Deus vocat, & peccatores renuunt, despiciuntque omne consilium Dei.
english: Thesis LXXXIII. This is Molina's express teaching in question 14, article 13, disputation 12: 'It can happen,' he says, 'that of two people inwardly called by God with equal aid, one is converted through the freedom of his choice and the other remains in unbelief. It often happens, too, that one person is converted with the same aid with which another is not.

'Indeed it can happen that someone anticipated and called with far greater aid is, in his freedom, not converted, while another is converted with far less. For God often calls, and sinners refuse and scorn all God's counsel.'

source_text: LXXXIV. Hinc patet nullo modo Molinae laborandum esse, ut efficaciam gratiae divinae cum arbitrii humani libertate conciliet. Siquidem Dei gratiam libero hominis arbitrio subjicit; nec vult ullum ejus auxilium esse tantae efficacitatis, ut liberum arbitrium ad agendum ex se determinet; sed qualecunque Dei auxilium ad bonam actionem praevium supponatur, cum eo semper stare posse voluntatis humanae dissensum, & in hominis potestate manere illo pro libitu uti, vel non uti.
english: Thesis LXXXIV. Plainly, then, Molina has no need to labour at reconciling the efficacy of divine grace with the freedom of human choice. He makes God's grace subject to man's free choice, and will not allow any aid of grace to be so efficacious that it determines free choice to act of itself.
Whatever aid from God is supposed to precede a good action, the human will's dissent can always coexist with it, and it remains in a person's power to use it as he pleases or not to use it.

source_text: LXXXV. Nihilominus vult actum liberi arbitrii quo gratiae divinae consentit, non esse mere naturalem, sed supernaturalem; & gratiae Dei tribui debere; Idque non solum quatenus dicitur praeveniens, & hominem allicit & invitat ad bonum, eique quodammodo novas vires sufficit: sed etiam quatenus per eandem gratiam, Deus cum libero hominis arbitrio in actum illius influit, quo respectu dicitur gratia coadjuvans. Nempe, ex ipsius mente, gratia illa Dei qua Deus hominem praevenit, voluntatem in agendo juvat, & cum ea cooperatur, qua ratione habitus potentiae inhaerens, cum illa ad actum ipsius concurrit. Ac proinde illa ipsa gratiae cooperatio a libera voluntate pendet, nec concipi debet ut voluntatem movens & ejus actione prior: quemadmodum influxus habitus in actum aliquem a potentia pendet, nec potentiam ad operandum movet, sed potentia se ad agendum movente simul cum ea in actum potentiae influit.
english: Thesis LXXXV. Even so, he holds that the act of free choice by which it consents to divine grace is not merely natural but supernatural, and must be ascribed to God's grace. This is so not only insofar as grace is called prevenient, alluring and inviting a person to the good and in a way supplying him with new strength, but also insofar as through that same grace God, together with man's free choice, flows into its act; in this respect it is called cooperating grace.

On his view, the grace by which God anticipates a person helps the will in acting and cooperates with it in the way a habit inhering in a power concurs with that power toward its act. So this cooperation of grace itself depends on the free will, and must not be thought of as moving the will or as prior to its action. In the same way, a habit's influence on an act depends on the power: the habit does not move the power to act, but, as the power moves itself to act, the habit flows together with it into the power's act.

source_text: LXXXVI. Sic hac de re Philosophatur Molina variis in locis. Praesertim vero disputatione quadragesima ad articulum 13. quaestionis 14. Tertio asseveramus, inquit, praevenientem gratiam, qua arbitrium adulti a spiritu sancto praevenitur, excitatur, allicitur, ac invitatur ad praedictos credendi, sperandi, diligendi, ac poenitendi actus, esse instrumentum spiritus sancti, quo ulterius efficienter concurrit ac influit cum arbitrio ipso, ad eosdem actus producendos, quando arbitrium ipsum praedictae gratiae consentit, & cum ea influit & cooperatur eosdem actus. Quare ejusmodi actus simul sunt efficienter ab arbitrio ipso per suum in eos influxum, & a Deo qui novo influxu, novave actione per praevenientem gratiam, tanquam per instrumentum in eosdem influit. Sicut enim habitus tam naturales quam supernaturales virtutum, quia inclinant potentias ad actus, habilesque proinde ad illos eas reddunt, concurrunt cum eis efficienter ad actus, suo partiali ac proprio influxu in eos influendo: ita cum gratia praeveniens alliciat, invitet, & inclinet potentias ad supernaturales illos actus eliciendos, utique quando potentiae consentiunt gratiae excitanti, in actusque influunt, ad quos gratia allicit & invitat, ipsamet etiam gratia influet & cooperabitur cum potentiis eosdem actus. Porro sicut, quod existat in rerum natura influxus habituum ad actus virtutum, quos potentiae eliciunt, pendet ab influxu ipsarummet potentiarum ad eosdem actus; eo quod habitus sufficiens causa non sit sine potentiarum concursu ad tales actus producendos: ita quod in rerum natura existat novus ille influxus gratiae praevenientis in actus credendi, sperandi, diligendi, ac poenitendi, pendet a cooperatione & influxu liberi nostri arbitrii in eosdem actus per intellectum & voluntatem; eo quod similiter gratia praeveniens causa sufficiens non sit eorundem actuum sine nostri arbitrii in eos cooperatione ac influxu.
english: Thesis LXXXVI. This is how Molina reasons on the matter in various places, but above all in disputation 40 on question 14, article 13: 'Third, we assert that prevenient grace, by which the Holy Spirit anticipates, rouses, allures and invites an adult's choice to the acts of believing, hoping, loving and repenting just mentioned, is an instrument of the Holy Spirit, by which he further concurs efficiently and flows in together with choice itself to produce those acts, when choice consents to that grace and, with it, flows into and cooperates in those acts. Such acts therefore come at once efficiently from choice itself, through its own influence on them, and from God, who flows into them by a new influence or new action through prevenient grace as through an instrument.

'For just as the habits of the virtues, natural and supernatural alike, incline the powers to their acts and so make them apt for them, and therefore concur efficiently with the powers toward those acts by flowing into them with their own partial influence, so, since prevenient grace allures, invites and inclines the powers to elicit those supernatural acts, whenever the powers consent to rousing grace and flow into the acts to which grace allures and invites them, grace itself will also flow in and cooperate with the powers in those acts.

'Again, just as the actual existence of the habits' influence on the acts of virtue that the powers elicit depends on the powers' own influence on those acts, since a habit is not a sufficient cause for producing such acts without the powers' concurrence, so the actual existence of that new influence of prevenient grace on the acts of believing, hoping, loving and repenting depends on the cooperation and influence of our free choice on those acts through intellect and will, since prevenient grace likewise is not a sufficient cause of those acts without our choice's cooperation in them and influence on them.'

source_text: LXXXVII. Unde fieri pertendit, Ut consensus liberi arbitrii Deo excitanti & vocanti per gratiam praevenientem, nihil in re sit quod non sit supernaturale, & quod non simul a Deo emanet, non solum tanquam ab alliciente, excitante & invitante ad id arbitrium, sed etiam tanquam a cooperante per auxilium gratiae. Ac proinde, ex ipsius sententia, Anathema censeri debet, qui affirmaverit consensum arbitrii nostri Deo excitanti & vocanti per auxilium gratiae praevenientis esse actum naturalem, aut posse elici sine auxilio & cooperatione ejusdem praevenientis gratiae. Quanquam iterum pronunciet esse etiam Anathema, qui dixerit eundem consensum non esse in libera arbitrii nostri ad modum ab ipso explicatum potestate: ita scilicet, ut sit penes liberum arbitrium, reddere cassam aut non reddere ejusmodi praevenientem spiritus sancti gratiam: quae sunt verba ejus in eadem quadragesima disputatione.
english: Thesis LXXXVII. From this he concludes that the consent of free choice to God, who rouses and calls through prevenient grace, is nothing in reality that is not supernatural and does not at the same time come from God, not only as from one who allures, rouses and invites choice to it, but also as from one who cooperates through the aid of grace. On his view, therefore, 'anyone who affirms that the consent of our choice to God, who rouses and calls through the aid of prevenient grace, is a natural act, or can be elicited without the aid and cooperation of that prevenient grace, must be held anathema.'

Yet he declares in turn that 'anyone is also anathema who says that this consent is not in the free power of our choice in the way he has explained', namely so that it lies with free choice to make such prevenient grace of the Holy Spirit void or not. These are his words in the same disputation 40.

source_text: LXXXVIII. Quae sint vero gratiae, & liberi arbitrii partes, circa bonos illos actus, in quibus consistit hominis conversio, distinctius explicat disputatione 37. ad eundem articulum. Ubi postquam supposuit ad bonum quemlibet actum haec tria concurrere; primo concursum generalem Dei ut primi agentis; secundo particularem gratiae divinae influxum; ac denique liberum hominis arbitrium: docet actum aliquem bonum, ut, exempli gratia, actum credendi, sperandi, poenitendi, a concursu Dei generali habere ut sit actus aliquis, non tamen hic potius quam ille: a libero arbitrio ut, quoad substantiam, sit actus hic & non alius: denique a gratia ut sit actus supernaturalis. Etenim, inquit, a Deo influente per solum concursum generalem emanat ut a causa universali, a qua proinde non habet magis quod sit assensus credendi, aut dolor de peccatis, quam vel actus oppositus, vel actus cujusvis alterius potentiae. Ab influxu vero liberi arbitrii, una cum notitiis & caeteris necessariis, ut quoad substantiam actus producatur, habet tanquam a causa particulari, ut, quoad substantiam actus, sit potius assensus fidei, aut dolor de peccatis, quam aliquis alius diversus actus. A gratia vero praeveniente, seu a Deo ut per illam tanquam per suum instrumentum una cum libero arbitrio influit in eundem actum, habet ut sit actus supernaturalis, specie distinctus ab actu pure naturali credendi, aut dolendi de peccatis, quem liberum arbitrium suis solis viribus tunc eliceret, si cum eo non influeret simul gratia praeveniens.
english: Thesis LXXXVIII. He explains more precisely what grace contributes and what free choice contributes to the good acts in which a person's conversion consists in disputation 37 on the same article. There he assumes that three things concur in any good act: first, God's general concurrence as first agent; second, the particular influence of divine grace; and finally, man's free choice.

He then teaches that a good act, for example the act of believing, hoping or repenting, has from God's general concurrence that it is an act at all, but not that it is this act rather than that one; from free choice, that in its substance it is this act and not another; and from grace, that it is a supernatural act.

'For,' he says, 'it comes from God, flowing in through the general concurrence alone, as from a universal cause, and so it has from that cause no more reason to be an assent of belief or sorrow for sins than to be the opposite act or an act of some other power. From the influence of free choice, together with the knowledge and other things needed for the act to be produced in its substance, it has, as from a particular cause, that in the substance of the act it is an assent of faith or sorrow for sins rather than some other act.

'From prevenient grace, that is, from God as he flows into the same act through it, as through his instrument, together with free choice, it has that it is a supernatural act, specifically distinct from the purely natural act of believing or of sorrowing for sins that free choice would then elicit by its own strength alone, if prevenient grace did not flow in together with it.'

source_text: LXXXIX. Igitur, ex illius mente, gratia Dei & liberum hominis arbitrium sunt duae partes unius integrae causae actus credendi, sperandi, aut poenitendi, prout ad salutem oportet; singulique ejusmodi actus pendent ab influxu tam liberi arbitrii, quam gratiae divinae: atque a libero quidem arbitrio habent, ut quoad substantiam sint credere, sperare, poenitere; ab influxu vero gratiae, ut sint supernaturales, & quales ad salutem sunt necessarii. Adeoque quivis eorum actuum, totus est a libero arbitrio, & totus a gratia: sed a neutro est ut a tota & integra causa, verum ut a parte integrae causae. Prout autor ille suam sententiam exponit, initio jamjam citatae disputationis.
english: Thesis LXXXIX. On his view, then, God's grace and man's free choice are two parts of one complete cause of the act of believing, hoping or repenting as salvation requires it, and each such act depends on the influence both of free choice and of divine grace. From free choice they have that in their substance they are believing, hoping and repenting; from the influence of grace, that they are supernatural and of the kind needed for salvation.

So each of these acts is wholly from free choice and wholly from grace, but from neither as from the whole and complete cause, only as from a part of the complete cause. This is how that author sets out his view at the beginning of the disputation just cited.
